meta.title: megascope — where the line is
meta.headline: Now the rules, and where they stop
meta.lede: Round 1 settled two things: this change is about posture rather than pre-filling, and it ships as two releases inside one tool. Your answer in your own words opened rules round 1 never asked about, so this round is written from the published guidance on planning before building rather than from my guesses. Two slots are open — where the line sits, and the rules we work inside.
meta.overallNotesHint: Same as last time: whatever you write here outranks every option above, and it sets the next round rather than being argued with.
meta.closingAsk: Update the line and the rules from these answers, then tell me what is still open.

constraints.label: The failure is posture
constraints.text: Not pre-filling itself — being cast as a reviewer when only you know the answer.

constraints.label: Discovery is its own page
constraints.text: A round zero of open questions, built by the same engine, with nothing pre-selected.

constraints.label: Two kinds of question
constraints.text: Narrowing questions arrive pre-answered; questions that open new ground arrive open.

constraints.label: The scope phase ends at the gate
constraints.text: Design is entered in a fresh session that loads only the hand-off.

constraints.label: Design gets its own rounds
constraints.text: A second loop, the same machinery, with its own set of slots.

constraints.label: Two releases, open page first
constraints.text: The opening page and the suggestion change ship before the gate and the design loop.

constraints.label: A brief plus a frozen log
constraints.text: What crosses the gate is the brief and a fixed list of decisions beside their answers.

constraints.label: The page shell carries no data
constraints.text: Personality arrives only through the theme, and a run generates only the data file.

constraints.label: Only the installed folder ships
constraints.text: Anything above it is missing at run time, so nothing shipped may point at it.

context.title: What the published guidance says
context.note: This round is written from the published guidance on planning before building rather than from my own instincts. These four findings shaped the questions below; none of them is itself a question.

items.desc: Finish the specification, then start a fresh session to execute it, so the new one carries clean context and nothing else.
Ask one question at a time, and put the questions whose answers would change the shape of the thing first.
If you can describe the whole change in one sentence, skip the plan. Planning earns its cost on uncertainty and breadth.
Current models check their own work, and telling them to verify makes them over-check. Give them something runnable instead.

scope.label: What we're trying to achieve
scope.text: Stop a run answering before it has listened. Discovery opens with real open questions, later rounds narrow with grounded suggestions, and the scope phase ends at a gate so design starts in a fresh session.

scope.label: What we hand over
scope.text: Two releases inside this one tool: first the open page and the suggestion change, then the gate and a design loop whose depth follows the size of the job. A brief plus a frozen list of decisions crosses the gate.

scope.label: What's in, and what's out
scope.text: Now that we know what we hand over, the line can be drawn: what the design phase owns, what the first release leaves alone, and whether the agreement-versus-silence fault gets fixed here.
scope.reopened: The deliverable is settled, so the line between this change and the design phase can finally be asked about properly.

scope.label: How we know it's done
scope.text: Assumed for now: the existing suite stays the gate for the machinery, and a real browser is what proves a new page works. What would convince you the change succeeded is the last round.
scope.assumption: The repository already treats its suite as the gate, so that is the honest default until you say what would actually convince you.

scope.label: What we work inside
scope.text: Your own words set working rules that need pinning down: how deep a design goes, how deferred features survive the hand-off, and what shape a done-test has to take.
scope.reopened: Your answer in your own words introduced working rules that round 1 never asked about.

glossary.megascope.mjs: the small zero-dependency program that checks a round's data file and builds the page

questions.context: Your own words said design depth should follow complexity: small and simple gets a build prompt, larger gets a real design. That only works if something decides which is which — and it has to be a test either of us can apply.
breakdown: A test you can apply yourself keeps the decision from being mine to make each time.
Too low a bar and small jobs drag a design phase they do not need.
Too high a bar and a genuinely uncertain change goes straight to building.
questions.question: What decides whether a job gets a design pass or just a build prompt?
questions.why: It is the only test here that came from outside, and it is checkable rather than a judgment call each time. What it misses is uncertainty: a one-line change in code you do not know still needs a plan.
questions.switchIf: Pick the second if you would rather design whenever the approach is unclear, even when the change itself is one line.

options.label: One sentence describes the change
options.detail: If you can state the whole change in one sentence, skip design and hand over a build prompt. Anything longer gets a design pass.

options.label: Uncertainty, not size
options.detail: Design whenever the approach is unclear or the code is unfamiliar, however small the change; skip it when you already know how.

options.label: The scope rounds decide
options.detail: If the line or the done-test needed more than one round to settle, the job is complicated enough to earn a design pass.

questions.context: Your answers this round showed something. Four of the six arrived pre-filled and were never actually opened, yet they exported as though you had agreed to them. The page cannot tell agreement from silence.
breakdown: It is the same fault as the posture problem, one layer down in how answers get recorded.
Fixing it touches the export that later rounds are checked against.
Leaving it means the first release still cannot tell agreement from silence.
questions.question: Should this change also fix agreement being confused with silence?
questions.why: It is the mechanism behind the failure you picked as primary, and the fix is small enough to ride along with the suggestion change. The cost is a wider first release and a changed export.
questions.switchIf: Pick the second if you want the first release as small as possible, and would rather record this and fix it on its own.

options.label: Fix it in the first release
options.detail: The export gains a way to say a pick was left alone rather than agreed to, so a later round cannot bank silence as evidence.

options.label: Record it, fix it separately
options.detail: Write it down as a known fault and keep the first release narrow. Simpler to ship, and the fault stays live meanwhile.

options.label: The open page makes it moot
options.detail: A page with nothing pre-selected cannot have untouched defaults. True of discovery, but the narrowing rounds still pre-fill.

questions.context: Today a run opens with a few questions in conversation before any page gets built. Once discovery is its own page of open questions, that conversation either goes away or has a much smaller job to do.
breakdown: Two places to ask opening questions is one more than the reader needs.
Something still has to decide how big the discovery page should be.
Whatever survives here is what a run does before you see anything at all.
questions.question: What happens to the questions asked in conversation before the page?
questions.why: Something has to size the page before it is written, and that is a small job better done in a sentence or two than in a document. The cost is that a run still opens with some conversation.
questions.switchIf: Pick the first if you want the page to be the very first thing you see, with nothing asked before it.

options.label: The page replaces it entirely
options.detail: A run reads your request, builds the discovery page, and asks nothing first. Simplest to follow, and it has to guess the size.

options.label: It shrinks to sizing the page
options.detail: One or two questions about what kind of job this is and how big, then the page. Nothing about the work itself is decided there.

options.label: It stays as it is
options.detail: Opening questions in conversation continue alongside the discovery page, and the two overlap by design.

questions.context: You said anything not simple and small should put the first version first and capture everything else for later. Where those captured items live decides whether they survive the hand-off or quietly vanish.
breakdown: Out of scope and deferred until later are two different promises to a reader.
A deferred item nobody records is indistinguishable from one that was rejected.
Whoever picks the work up later needs to know which of the two it was.
questions.question: Where do features deferred to a later version get recorded?
questions.why: Something ruled out and something agreed for later read identically if they share a heading, and the second is the one a later session needs to find. The cost is one more section to keep in step.
questions.switchIf: Pick the first if you would rather keep the hand-off short and can live with one heading covering both.

options.label: The existing in-and-out section
options.detail: Deferred items sit with everything else that is out, marked as deferred. Fewer moving parts, and the two blur together.

options.label: Its own section in the hand-off
options.detail: A named list of what was agreed for later, kept apart from what was ruled out, so a later session can pick it straight up.

options.label: It becomes the next scope
options.detail: Deferred items are the opening material for the next run of this tool, rather than a list inside the current hand-off.

questions.context: The published guidance pulls two ways. Give the agent a check it can actually run — but do not tell it to verify, because the current models already do that, and asking makes them over-check for nothing.
breakdown: A runnable check closes the loop without you having to watch it.
Not every job has one, because a plan has no command to run.
An instruction to double-check costs tokens and buys nothing back.
questions.example: For code, a command that exits zero: `node assets/megascope.mjs ready docs/scoping/megascope-phases/`. For a plan there is none, so the test is whether a fresh session can start unaided.
questions.question: What shape must the done-test take in the hand-off?
questions.why: Tying the shape to the kind of work we already record means neither arm is a hedge: code owes a command, a plan owes a stated test. Demanding a command everywhere would just produce fake ones.
questions.switchIf: Pick the first if you want one hard bar, and would rather refuse to close a scope that cannot name a command.

options.label: A command returning pass or fail
options.detail: The slot must name something runnable. Hardest bar, and it cannot be met when the thing handed over is a plan.

options.label: A plain-language done test
options.detail: A sentence a person can check. Always writable, and it leaves the agent with nothing it can run on its own.

options.label: Keyed to the kind of work
options.detail: A command when the hand-over is code; a stated test when it is a plan. The kind is already recorded, so the rule can follow it.

questions.context: You asked what the guidance says about models. The durable part is effort — how hard to think — because model names change. So the question is whether the hand-off names either of them at all.
breakdown: A named model is wrong the moment a better one ships.
An effort level is advice that survives, and it is the main cost lever.
Naming neither leaves the choice to whoever runs the work.
questions.question: Does the hand-off say how hard to think, or stay silent?
questions.why: Effort is the lever the guidance actually emphasises, and it does not rot the way a model name does. The cost is a line in every hand-off that some readers will ignore.
questions.switchIf: Pick the third if you want the hand-off fully self-contained, and accept editing it whenever a new model lands.

options.label: It says nothing
options.detail: Whoever runs the work chooses. Nothing to keep current, and a demanding job may quietly get a shallow pass.

options.label: How hard to think, only
options.detail: One line on how much effort the job deserves, with no model named. Survives new releases and is the main cost control.

options.label: Both the model and the effort
options.detail: Fully specified, so a fresh session needs no judgment. It also goes stale, and stale advice still reads as current.
